findings.title: Unpinned package executed on every start: toolrouter-mcp
findings.detail: 'toolrouter-mcp' launches toolrouter-mcp through npx without a version. The client resolves the version at start time, so any future publish to that package name runs with your credentials. This is how postmark-mcp (Sept 2025) reached roughly 300 organisations.
findings.remediation: Pin an exact version and an integrity hash: "args": ["toolrouter-mcp@<version>"] and drop the -y flag. Re-pin deliberately, after reviewing the diff.

findings.title: Description reads as instructions to the model (p=1.00): discover
findings.detail: The description of 'toolrouter-mcp.discover' scores 1.00 on the instruction-detection model, and carries intent signals: concealment. Descriptions are documentation for a human, but they are delivered to the model as trusted context, so text that tells the model what to do is an attack surface rather than a description. The score is driven mainly by: concealment, cross_tool, entropy, log_len.

evidence.description:
Find the right ToolRouter tool for your task. Describe what you need in plain language.
Examples: "analyze a website", "research competitors", "find prospect companies", "check DNS records".
Exact tool name (e.g. "seo") returns full schemas and examples.
Flow: prefer route({ intent }) to pick and run a tool. Use discover when you need schemas or a listing, then call use_tool(tool, skill, input).
Every discover response also includes a top-level `connectors` array listing SaaS accounts the user h

findings.remediation: Read the description against what the tool actually does. If the text is legitimate, it usually means the tool should not have to instruct the model at all - move the guidance into the parameter descriptions or the server's own docs.

findings.title: Toxic flow within 'toolrouter-mcp': reads credentials or secrets + sends email or messages
findings.detail: 7 combination(s) exist where one tool reads credentials or secrets and another sends email or messages. Neither tool is malicious on its own; together they reads credentials and can send mail. This is the postmark-mcp shape: the mail tool was legitimate, the credentials were reachable, and the combination was the incident. Both sides live in the same server, which may well be by design; confirm it.
findings.remediation: Break the path, not the tools: scope the credential so the source tool cannot reach anything valuable, or require explicit user confirmation on the sink tool (destructiveHint / human-in-the-loop), or split the two capabilities across trust boundaries that cannot share a context window.

findings.title: Toxic flow within 'toolrouter-mcp': executes commands + writes or deletes files
findings.detail: 4 combination(s) exist where one tool executes commands and another writes or deletes files. Neither tool is malicious on its own; together they executes commands and writes files, so the agent can persist a payload for a later session to pick up. Both sides live in the same server, which may well be by design; confirm it.
findings.remediation: Break the path, not the tools: scope the credential so the source tool cannot reach anything valuable, or require explicit user confirmation on the sink tool (destructiveHint / human-in-the-loop), or split the two capabilities across trust boundaries that cannot share a context window.

findings.title: No baseline supplied - drift detection is disabled
findings.detail: Without an approved snapshot the scanner cannot tell a tool that has always been there from one that appeared yesterday. The single most effective MCP control is the diff, and it needs a baseline to diff against.
findings.remediation: Run 'mcp-scrutiny baseline --config <file> --out mcp-baseline.json', commit the file, and pass it back with --baseline on every later scan.
